pattern: Scarce inventory under contention: make the claim on an item an atomic, expiring lease in the source of truth, gate a stampede with admission control before it reaches the database, and finish with an idempotent external payment that confirms the lease.

checks.label: Discovery use case captured

tips.nudge: Before anyone buys, what do most visitors actually do?
tips.hint: Add a functional requirement for finding events and looking at one.
tips.show: F1: Browse and search events by name, performer, city and date; view an event page.

checks.label: Seat selection use case captured

tips.nudge: A fan picks seats, then types card details for a few minutes. What protects the seats meanwhile?
tips.hint: Add a requirement for temporarily reserving chosen seats with a time limit.
tips.show: F3: Hold the selected seats for 10 minutes while the fan pays; the hold lapses automatically.

checks.label: Purchase use case captured

tips.nudge: What turns a held seat into a ticket?
tips.hint: Add a requirement for paying and getting a confirmed ticket.
tips.show: F4: Pay for held seats and receive a confirmed booking and e-ticket.

checks.label: Correctness guarantee for inventory stated

tips.nudge: Which failure would end up in the news?
tips.hint: State the consistency guarantee for seats as a non-functional requirement.
tips.show: N1: No double booking: each seat is sold at most once (strong consistency on inventory, even under contention).

checks.label: Traffic shape of a big sale addressed

tips.nudge: What happens at 10:00:00 when a stadium tour goes on sale?
tips.hint: Add a non-functional requirement about sudden demand far above supply, and fairness.
tips.show: N3: Survive on-sale spikes (≈10M fans for 50k seats within minutes) and admit fans fairly, roughly first come first served.

checks.label: Everyday read throughput estimated

tips.nudge: Start from daily users and the pages each one views.
tips.hint: browse_qps = DAU × page views per user / seconds per day.
tips.show: browse_qps = 10M × 20 / day ≈ 2,300 /s (peak ×5 ≈ 12k /s).

checks.label: Load of a single hot on-sale estimated

tips.nudge: How many fans arrive for one hot event, and over how long?
tips.hint: Arrival rate = fans who show up / the window they arrive in.
tips.show: onsale_arrival_qps = 10M fans / 600 s ≈ 17k /s, against only 50k seats (200 fans per seat).

checks.label: Inventory storage per year estimated

tips.nudge: The seat table is the big one. How many seat rows per year?
tips.hint: Seat rows = events per year × seats per event; × bytes per row.
tips.show: seat_storage_year = 100k events × 5k seats × 200 B ≈ 100 GB/year: fits a sharded or even single Postgres.

checks.label: Seat reservation endpoint defined

tips.nudge: What does the client send when the fan clicks 'reserve these seats'?
tips.hint: A POST that names the event and seats and returns a hold with an expiry, or a conflict.
tips.show: POST /events/{id}/holds {seat_ids} → 201 {hold_id, expires_at} | 409 seats taken

checks.label: Purchase endpoint defined

tips.nudge: How does a hold become a paid booking, and what if the client retries?
tips.hint: A POST that references the hold and a payment token; make it safe to retry.
tips.show: POST /bookings {hold_id, payment_token} + Idempotency-Key → 202 {booking_id, status: pending}

checks.label: Inventory modelled

tips.nudge: What row must exist per seat per event so that two fans can't both get it?
tips.hint: Model one row per (event, seat) with a status and who holds it until when.
tips.show: seats(event_id, seat_id, status available|held|sold, hold_id, held_until, booking_id, version) in Postgres.

checks.label: Inventory contention designed as its own part

tips.nudge: Two fans click the same seat in the same millisecond. Treat that as its own sub-problem.
tips.hint: Compare a DB row lock held for 10 minutes, a Redis lock with a TTL, and an atomic conditional update with an expiry column.
tips.show: Part 'Seat hold, no double booking': UPDATE seats SET status='held', held_until=now()+10m WHERE status='available' OR held_until < now(); all-or-nothing per request; expiry is checked lazily, so nothing has to release a hold.

checks.label: Demand far above supply designed as its own part

tips.nudge: 200 fans per seat arrive at once. Should all of them reach the booking service?
tips.hint: Compare autoscaling, rate limiting with 429s, and a virtual queue that admits fans at a fixed rate.
tips.show: Part 'Virtual waiting room': fans join a Redis sorted set by arrival time; an admitter lets N per second through with a signed, short-lived token that the gateway checks on hold/booking calls.

checks.label: Read path designed as its own part

tips.nudge: Most traffic is people looking, not buying. Give that its own part.
tips.hint: Compare querying the database directly with a search index plus caches/CDN.
tips.show: Part 'Browse and search': Elasticsearch fed by CDC for search, CDN + Redis for event pages, seat maps cached for a few seconds (the hold is the real check).

checks.label: Payment designed as its own part

tips.nudge: Paying talks to a third party that can be slow, fail, or answer twice. Give it its own part.
tips.hint: Compare charging inside the DB transaction with a pending booking that a PSP webhook confirms.
tips.show: Part 'Payment and confirmation': booking created pending with an idempotency key, PSP charge, webhook confirms → seats sold, outbox event issues the ticket.

checks.label: Read path can absorb the read load

tips.nudge: Event pages are identical for everyone. Why compute them per request?
tips.hint: Put something in front of the database for event pages and seat maps.
tips.show: CDN for static/event pages, Redis for event details and a seat-map snapshot with a short TTL.

checks.label: Traffic spread and gated at the edge

tips.nudge: Where would you check that a fan was admitted from the queue?
tips.hint: Put an entry point in front of the services that balances load and can enforce admission.
tips.show: API gateway / load balancer: routes to stateless services and rejects hold/booking calls without a valid admission token.

checks.label: Money handled by the right party

tips.nudge: Do you want card numbers in your database?
tips.hint: Delegate the charge to an outside provider and connect your booking service to it.
tips.show: Booking service → payment provider (Stripe/Adyen): create a charge with an idempotency key; the PSP calls back via webhook.

checks.label: How unpaid seats come back decided

tips.nudge: A fan closes the tab mid-checkout. When and how does the seat become available again?
tips.hint: Compare a cron sweeper, a Redis key TTL and checking the expiry at read time.
tips.show: Lazy expiry: a seat is free if status='available' OR held_until < now(); an optional sweeper tidies rows for the seat map. No job is needed for correctness.

checks.label: Retries and late payment results handled

tips.nudge: The PSP times out, the client retries, then the webhook arrives after the hold has expired. What happens?
tips.hint: Decide on idempotency keys and what to do with a payment that succeeds too late.
tips.show: Idempotency key per booking on our API and on the PSP call; confirming re-checks the hold with a conditional update; if the seats were lost, refund automatically.

checks.label: Bottlenecks and single points of failure named

tips.nudge: Which single row or shard gets hammered during a hot on-sale?
tips.hint: Walk the hold path for one event and name what saturates.
tips.show: One event's seats on one shard (contention), the waiting-room Redis, the PSP rate limits; mitigations: admission rate, partition by event, multi-PSP.

checks.label: Failure behaviour described

tips.nudge: The PSP is down for 2 minutes during a sale. What do fans see?
tips.hint: Describe what happens when the cache, the queue store and the PSP fail.
tips.show: Cache down → reads fall back to the DB behind the waiting room; PSP down → bookings stay pending, holds extended briefly, then released; queue Redis down → pause admissions, not sales in flight.
